pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of the church office in this workspace. Share it with the pastor, the administrator, the care coordinator, the worship lead and the facilities steward.
: every family, member and visitor, the people and children at home, their groups, giving and a follow-up date with a shepherd.
: services, classes, youth nights, meals, funerals, weddings and rentals, each in a room with its setup.
: every space with its capacity, rental rate, bookings and rental income.
: greeters, nursery, sound, kitchen and setup for each event, open or filled.
: visits, meals, rides and calls, confidential notes, and the prayer list.
: the weekly count in the room and online, first-time guests and the offering.
Monday: Sunday's counts and offering entered; visitors added and assigned.
Tuesday: the care meeting; requests assigned for the week.
Wednesday: next Sunday's volunteer roles filled; rentals for the weekend confirmed.
Friday: the facilities steward walks the room setups for the weekend.
Every morning: care requests due today and overdue
Every Monday: visitors to follow up, attendance entered
Every month: households who have not been seen, rental income, open volunteer roles
Every season: newcomers class and the attendance trend for the board
Care notes, phone numbers and giving are confidential. Share this workspace with staff and the care team only. Children's details stay minimal.

Rename gatherings, groups, rooms and volunteer areas to match your congregation and delete the sample rows once your own are in. Edit any cell in place, drag cards between columns, and every count updates on its own.
The community at a glance. Charts read the live tables.

text.text: The building is busy all week. One calendar, one person who says yes, and a written agreement for every outside group keeps it that way without double bookings or surprises.
Check the room on the Events calendar first. Look at the room's
Add the event with its room, lead, start time and the
The administrator confirms it within two days and sets it to
. Kitchen use always needs the facilities steward's yes.
Weddings, recitals, neighborhood meetings and family celebrations bring in income and new faces.
Rental agreement signed, with the date, hours, room and guest count
Proof of event insurance for groups over 50 people
Key or door code arranged with the facilities steward
Rules sent: no open flames, how to use the kitchen, when the building closes
Set one public rate per room and a lower rate for members and nonprofits. Funerals for members are never charged. Write the rate on the room so everyone quotes the same price.
The facilities steward walks the room list for the coming week and checks every setup.
Heating or cooling is set for the event times.
Volunteer roles for the event are filled or marked not needed.
Walk the room: damage, lost property, kitchen clean.
Return the deposit, or keep the part needed for repairs with a written note.

Services and funerals come first, then congregation events, then rentals. When a funeral needs a room that is rented, call the renter the same day and offer another room or date with an apology and a discount.

A couple asks for the fellowship hall for a reception of 95 guests. The administrator checks the calendar, sends the agreement, takes a deposit and records the $600 fee. Ten days before, the steward confirms round tables and a cleared dance floor; the hall's rental income for the quarter updates on its own.
Most first-time guests decide within ten minutes whether to come back, and most of that is decided in the parking lot and at the door. Welcome is a team's job, not just the pastor's.
Greeters at every door, ten minutes before and after the service.
A clear welcome table with a simple card asking only for a name and an email or phone.
Someone sits near new faces and walks them to coffee afterward. Do not single anyone out from the front.

Hold a short newcomers class each season: what the congregation believes, how it is run, how to serve and how to give. Those who join become

Families with children need to know their kids are safe. Check-in for children's rooms, two screened adults in every room, and a clear pickup rule. Record only what you need about children here, and never photographs.
Every visitor from Sunday has a note and a follow-up date

The Lindahl-Basu family visits with their toddler. A greeter shows them the nursery, someone sits with them, and they fill in a card. Monday, the administrator adds them as visitors; Tuesday, the pastor emails; two weeks later they join a small group and move to Exploring.
Care is the heart of congregational life, and it fails quietly when a request lives in one person's memory. Every request goes on the list, has a person and a date, and is closed when it is done.

Fifteen minutes with the pastor, care coordinator and a lay leader:
Overdue and today's requests: who is going?
Members who have not been seen in a month: who will call?
Requests done this week: mark them
After a death, plan care for a year, not a week: calls at one month, three months, the first holidays and the anniversary. Add each one as its own request with a date so none is forgotten.
Rotate visitors so nobody carries too much. Give the care team a place to talk after hard visits, with confidentiality.

Gus has knee surgery on Thursday. Pilar mentions it after the service. The care coordinator adds a meal request for Friday and a ride for his physical therapy, asks Pilar whether Gus would like to be on the prayer list (he would), and lines up three families for meals. Each request is marked done as it happens.
